title: Pakistan's Tariff Regime: Comparative Perspective
gist: Oxford Economics reassesses Pakistan's National Tariff Policy 2025–30 claim that Pakistan has the highest tariffs among peers and finds it mid-range: 9.5% simple MFN average (equal to Vietnam), 6.7% trade-weighted, and 17.7% including para-tariffs versus 28.1% for Bangladesh and 19.3% for Sri Lanka. With no clear link between tariff levels and export/GDP, it argues export strategy should prioritise competitiveness (energy, logistics, finance, skills) and carefully sequence tariff cuts to preserve negotiating leverage.

themes.theme: Pakistan customs duties sit mid-pack, not at the top

insights.claim: Oxford Economics' reassessment finds Pakistan's National Tariff Policy 2025–30 overstates its relative protection: on a consistent basis Pakistan's average customs duties fall in the middle of a 10-economy peer range (India, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Thailand, Cambodia, Indonesia, Vietnam, Türkiye).
insights.speaker: Jiawen Cui
insights.so_what: The official policy narrative that Pakistan is an outlier high-tariff economy may be driving reform priorities on a flawed premise.

themes.theme: Tariff peaks: moderately high duties, few extremes

insights.claim: In 2025, 31.0% of Pakistan's tariff lines carried duties above 15%, versus a five-country South Asian average of 30.7%, ranking Pakistan fourth of ten study economies.
insights.speaker: Jiawen Cui
insights.so_what: Pakistan's share of high-duty lines is essentially at the regional norm.

themes.theme: Para-tariffs reshape the ranking but don't make Pakistan the outlier

insights.claim: Including para-tariffs, Pakistan's estimated combined simple average of tariffs and para-tariffs is 17.7%, versus 28.1% for Bangladesh, 19.3% for Sri Lanka, 17.3% for Türkiye and 16.0% for India.
insights.speaker: Jiawen Cui
insights.so_what: Bangladesh and Sri Lanka carry heavier total import charges than Pakistan once para-tariffs are counted.
insights.quote: Its estimated combined simple average of tariffs and para-tariffs is 17.7%, compared with 28.1% for Bangladesh, 19.3% for Sri Lanka, 17.3% for Türkiye and 16.0% for India.

insights.claim: Cross-country tariff comparisons are only meaningful if para-tariffs are treated consistently across all economies; the NTP comparison's conclusion hinges on this methodological choice.
insights.speaker: Jiawen Cui
insights.so_what: Inconsistent inclusion of para-tariffs can manufacture an apparent outlier status.
insights.quote: Consistent treatment of these additional charges is therefore essential.

insights.claim: The combined tariff/para-tariff estimates are a best-effort comparison, limited by differences in data coverage, reference periods and policy changes, and not a comprehensive measure of all import charges.
insights.speaker: Jiawen Cui
insights.so_what: Readers should treat the para-tariff ranking as directional, not precise.

insights.claim: The data do not support the claim that Pakistan has the highest tariff levels among the economies compared.

insights.claim: Across the study economies there is no clear correlation between simple average tariff rate and exports as a share of GDP.
insights.speaker: Jiawen Cui
insights.so_what: Cutting tariffs alone is unlikely to lift Pakistan's export intensity.

insights.claim: Pakistan's export strategy should rest on how reform improves export competitiveness rather than on tariff reduction alone; tariff reform must sit within a broader package covering energy, logistics, finance and skills.
insights.speaker: Jiawen Cui
insights.so_what: Binding constraints on Pakistani exporters are likely energy, logistics, finance and skills costs rather than input tariffs.

insights.so_what: Unilateral liberalisation now could forfeit negotiating leverage in a protectionist world; tariffs retain strategic value as trade-deal currency.
